text: TR is measured from:
options: The start of the scan to the end of the scan
One excitation pulse to the next excitation of the same slice
The end of readout to the next RF pulse
The excitation pulse to the center of the echo
explanation: TR is the repetition time between successive excitations.
source_note: Original study-bank question based on Chapter 1 MRI principles. Review before publishing.

text: TE is measured from:
options: The start to the end of the scan
One excitation pulse to the next
The excitation pulse to the center of the echo
The end of the echo to the next RF pulse
explanation: TE is the time from excitation to the middle of the echo or signal.
source_note: Original study-bank question based on Chapter 1 MRI principles. Review before publishing.

text: In which units are TR and TE normally expressed?
explanation: TR and TE are times, typically in milliseconds.
source_note: Original study-bank question based on Chapter 1 MRI principles. Review before publishing.

text: TE is normally longer than TR.
explanation: The echo occurs within each repetition period, so TE is shorter than TR.
source_note: Original study-bank question based on Chapter 1 MRI principles. Review before publishing.

text: A very short TR means that between excitations the longitudinal magnetization has:
explanation: A short TR limits T1 recovery.
source_note: Original study-bank question based on Chapter 1 MRI principles. Review before publishing.

text: A long TR allows the longitudinal magnetization to:
explanation: A longer interval gives more time for the magnetization to return toward equilibrium.
source_note: Original study-bank question based on Chapter 1 MRI principles. Review before publishing.

text: A short TE means that, when the signal is measured, the transverse magnetization:
options: Has had little time to decay
explanation: There is little time for T2 decay before measurement.
source_note: Original study-bank question based on Chapter 1 MRI principles. Review before publishing.

text: A long TE means that, when the signal is measured, the transverse magnetization has:
explanation: More time passes for dephasing before the echo is sampled.
source_note: Original study-bank question based on Chapter 1 MRI principles. Review before publishing.

text: A sequence has TR = 400 ms. How long do five TR periods last?
source_note: Original study-bank question based on Chapter 1 MRI principles. Review before publishing.

text: A scan uses TR = 2,000 ms. How many TR periods fit in one minute?
source_note: Original study-bank question based on Chapter 1 MRI principles. Review before publishing.

text: Convert a TR of 0.5 s into milliseconds.
source_note: Original study-bank question based on Chapter 1 MRI principles. Review before publishing.

text: Convert a TE of 20 ms into seconds.
source_note: Original study-bank question based on Chapter 1 MRI principles. Review before publishing.

text: A sequence repeats every 600 ms for 128 repetitions. What is the total time, ignoring other factors?
source_note: Original study-bank question based on Chapter 1 MRI principles. Review before publishing.

text: In a standard sequence, TR must be longer than TE.
explanation: The echo is formed within each repetition period.
source_note: Original study-bank question based on Chapter 1 MRI principles. Review before publishing.

text: A shorter TR generally allows a shorter scan time, other factors being equal.
explanation: Each repetition takes less time, so the scan finishes sooner.
source_note: Original study-bank question based on Chapter 1 MRI principles. Review before publishing.

text: Increasing TR while keeping other factors equal will generally:
explanation: Scan time is proportional to TR.
source_note: Original study-bank question based on Chapter 1 MRI principles. Review before publishing.

text: Which combination leaves the least longitudinal magnetization available for the next excitation?
options: Any flip angle with a long TR
A small flip angle with a long TR
A zero flip angle with any TR
A large flip angle with a short TR
explanation: A large flip angle uses up much longitudinal magnetization, and a short TR allows little recovery.
source_note: Original study-bank question based on Chapter 1 MRI principles. Review before publishing.

text: Compared with a 90 degree pulse, a small flip angle leaves:
explanation: A smaller flip angle tips less magnetization, so more remains along Z.
source_note: Original study-bank question based on Chapter 1 MRI principles. Review before publishing.

text: Why can a small flip angle allow a short TR to be used?
options: Less longitudinal magnetization is lost at each excitation, so less recovery is needed
explanation: Less magnetization is tipped, so the longitudinal component recovers sufficiently within a short TR.
source_note: Original study-bank question based on Chapter 1 MRI principles. Review before publishing.

text: The angle through which RF rotates the net magnetization is the:
explanation: The flip angle describes how far the net magnetization is tipped.
source_note: Original study-bank question based on Chapter 1 MRI principles. Review before publishing.

text: Which pair of parameters basically determines how much recovery and decay occur before and during signal measurement?
explanation: TR controls the recovery time and TE controls the decay time.
source_note: Original study-bank question based on Chapter 1 MRI principles. Review before publishing.

text: A scan uses a very short TR and a very short TE. Which is true when the signal is measured?
options: Longitudinal recovery was limited and little transverse decay occurred
explanation: A short TR limits recovery and a short TE limits decay.
source_note: Original study-bank question based on Chapter 1 MRI principles. Review before publishing.

text: A technologist doubles TR from 500 ms to 1,000 ms, all else equal. What happens to scan time?
explanation: Scan time is proportional to TR.
source_note: Original study-bank question based on Chapter 1 MRI principles. Review before publishing.

text: A technologist halves TE and changes nothing else. What happens to the T2 decay that occurs before measurement?
explanation: A shorter TE leaves less time for dephasing.
source_note: Original study-bank question based on Chapter 1 MRI principles. Review before publishing.

text: TR is shortened substantially. What is the effect on the longitudinal magnetization at the next excitation?
options: It is lower, because recovery is incomplete
explanation: With less recovery time, less magnetization is available.
source_note: Original study-bank question based on Chapter 1 MRI principles. Review before publishing.

text: The time between excitations most directly affects which relaxation process?
explanation: TR sets the time allowed for longitudinal recovery.
source_note: Original study-bank question based on Chapter 1 MRI principles. Review before publishing.

text: Echo time most directly affects which relaxation process?
explanation: TE sets the time allowed for transverse decay before sampling.
source_note: Original study-bank question based on Chapter 1 MRI principles. Review before publishing.

text: Which statement about relaxation times in tissue is generally correct?
explanation: T1 values are generally several times longer than T2 values in tissue.
source_note: Original study-bank question based on Chapter 1 MRI principles. Review before publishing.

text: Which of the following is not a time interval?
explanation: Flip angle is an angle. The others are times.
source_note: Original study-bank question based on Chapter 1 MRI principles. Review before publishing.

text: The flip angle is measured in degrees.
explanation: The flip angle is an angle of rotation.
source_note: Original study-bank question based on Chapter 1 MRI principles. Review before publishing.

text: Which is the correct order of events in a basic MR experiment?
options: RF excitation, alignment in B0, relaxation, detection
Alignment in B0, RF excitation, then signal detection while relaxation occurs
explanation: The nuclei first align in B0. RF then excites them, and the signal is detected as the magnetization relaxes.
source_note: Original study-bank question based on Chapter 1 MRI principles. Review before publishing.

text: Select all factors that affect the equilibrium net magnetization.
options: The number of hydrogen nuclei per unit volume
The position of the receive coil
The flip angle of the next pulse
explanation: Net magnetization depends on the population excess (set by B0) and the number of nuclei.
source_note: Original study-bank question based on Chapter 1 MRI principles. Review before publishing.

text: Select all that occur during RF excitation at resonance.
options: The magnetic moments are brought into phase
The net magnetization is tipped away from B0
explanation: Resonance transfers energy, brings moments into phase and tips the net magnetization.
source_note: Original study-bank question based on Chapter 1 MRI principles. Review before publishing.

text: Select all true statements about the signal in the receive coil.
options: It is induced by a changing magnetic flux
It decays as the transverse magnetization decays
It is produced by longitudinal magnetization at equilibrium
It oscillates at the Larmor frequency
It is independent of the transverse magnetization
explanation: The signal comes from rotating transverse magnetization and decays as that magnetization decays.
source_note: Original study-bank question based on Chapter 1 MRI principles. Review before publishing.

text: Select all true statements about MR active nuclei.
options: They contain an unpaired proton or neutron
explanation: MR active nuclei have unpaired nucleons, which give net spin and a magnetic moment.
source_note: Original study-bank question based on Chapter 1 MRI principles. Review before publishing.

text: Select all quantities that are measured in units of time.
explanation: TR and TE are times. The others are an angle, a field strength and a frequency per tesla.
source_note: Original study-bank question based on Chapter 1 MRI principles. Review before publishing.

text: Which statement correctly links field strength, frequency and signal?
options: A higher field raises the Larmor frequency and the net magnetization
A higher field raises frequency but lowers net magnetization
explanation: Larmor frequency and population excess both rise with B0.
source_note: Original study-bank question based on Chapter 1 MRI principles. Review before publishing.

text: A scanner is upgraded from 1.5 T to 3 T. Which of the following must change for hydrogen imaging?
options: The number of protons in hydrogen
explanation: Hydrogen's properties are fixed, but its Larmor frequency doubles.
source_note: Original study-bank question based on Chapter 1 MRI principles. Review before publishing.

text: A phantom is in the scanner and no RF has been applied. What is the net magnetization?
options: Longitudinal and static, so no signal is detected
explanation: Without excitation, the net magnetization stays along B0 and induces no signal.
source_note: Original study-bank question based on Chapter 1 MRI principles. Review before publishing.

text: RF at the Larmor frequency of phosphorus-31 is accidentally applied while hydrogen is being imaged at 1.5 T. What is the effect on hydrogen?
explanation: Phosphorus precesses at a much lower frequency than hydrogen, so the RF does not match hydrogen's resonance.
source_note: Original study-bank question based on Chapter 1 MRI principles. Review before publishing.

text: At 1.5 T, what is the approximate Larmor frequency of phosphorus-31 (gyromagnetic ratio 17.25 MHz/T)?
source_note: Original study-bank question based on Chapter 1 MRI principles. Review before publishing.

text: Fluorine-19 has a gyromagnetic ratio of about 40.05 MHz/T. What is its approximate Larmor frequency at 3 T?
source_note: Original study-bank question based on Chapter 1 MRI principles. Review before publishing.

text: Sodium-23 has a gyromagnetic ratio of about 11.26 MHz/T. What is its approximate Larmor frequency at 3 T?
source_note: Original study-bank question based on Chapter 1 MRI principles. Review before publishing.

text: At a given field strength, hydrogen and phosphorus-31 nuclei precess at the same frequency.
explanation: Each nucleus has its own gyromagnetic ratio, so they precess at different frequencies.
source_note: Original study-bank question based on Chapter 1 MRI principles. Review before publishing.

text: Why is MR described as a resonance phenomenon?
options: The scanner vibrates at the Larmor frequency
Nuclei absorb energy efficiently only from RF at their Larmor frequency
explanation: Resonance means efficient energy transfer at the matching frequency.
source_note: Original study-bank question based on Chapter 1 MRI principles. Review before publishing.

text: Which best defines relaxation in MR?
options: The return of the magnetization to equilibrium after excitation
The application of the RF pulse
The alignment of nuclei in B0
explanation: Relaxation involves T1 recovery and T2 decay after excitation.
source_note: Original study-bank question based on Chapter 1 MRI principles. Review before publishing.

text: When does the MR signal begin to be generated?
options: When transverse magnetization is created by excitation
As soon as the patient enters the room
explanation: Signal needs transverse magnetization, which only exists after RF excitation.
source_note: Original study-bank question based on Chapter 1 MRI principles. Review before publishing.

text: Which sequence best describes how an MR signal is created?
options: Nuclei emit gamma rays that are counted
RF is reflected from the nuclei
Net magnetization is tipped into the transverse plane, precesses, and induces a voltage in the coil
explanation: The signal comes from electromagnetic induction by precessing transverse magnetization.
source_note: Original study-bank question based on Chapter 1 MRI principles. Review before publishing.

text: What is the main difference between the roles of B0 and B1?
options: Both rotate at the Larmor frequency
B0 aligns the nuclei, while B1 is applied briefly to excite them
B0 excites the nuclei and B1 aligns them
explanation: B0 is the static main field and B1 is the RF field used in pulses.
source_note: Original study-bank question based on Chapter 1 MRI principles. Review before publishing.

text: B1 is a static magnetic field.
explanation: B1 is an oscillating RF field. B0 is the static field.
source_note: Original study-bank question based on Chapter 1 MRI principles. Review before publishing.

text: Why does hydrogen MRI use RF in the tens to hundreds of MHz?
options: RF below 1 MHz cannot enter the body
Larmor frequencies at clinical field strengths lie in that range
explanation: For hydrogen, 0.5 to 7 T corresponds to roughly 21 to 298 MHz.
source_note: Original study-bank question based on Chapter 1 MRI principles. Review before publishing.
